title: Indian Applicants to US Law Schools Have Dropped 23 Per Cent. The Visa Climate Is Driving Them Away.
excerpt: America denied 35 per cent of international student visa applications last year — the highest rate in a decade. Indian LL.M. applicants are increasingly choosing the UK and Europe instead.
body:
Indian applications to Master of Laws programmes at American law schools have fallen 23 per cent this year, part of a broader retreat by international students from a country that once rolled out the welcome mat for them.

The decline is not confined to India. Chinese applicants dropped 21 per cent. The overall international LL.M. applicant pool shrank 14 per cent, according to data from the Law School Admission Council, which tracks admissions at most U.S. law schools. But India's slide is among the sharpest — and it is happening at a moment when the country produces more outbound graduate students than almost any other nation on Earth.

"There is a feeling that the United States, generally speaking, is maybe not as welcoming to international students as it used to be," said Gisele Joachim, the Council's vice president for law school engagement.

## The Numbers at Elite Schools

The decline is not abstract. At the University of California, Berkeley School of Law, LL.M. applications are down 20 per cent. Assistant admissions dean Joseph Lindsay said he is "doubtful" the school will meet its fall target of 240 LL.M. students. At the University of Michigan Law School, the drop is 30 per cent — on top of an 8 per cent decline the previous year.

Columbia, New York University, Harvard, and Georgetown — schools with the largest LL.M. programmes — all declined to discuss their numbers with Reuters. Their silence speaks to a sector-wide anxiety: international students are a critical revenue stream, paying full tuition with little financial aid, and the pipeline is thinning.

The average tuition for an LL.M. at a private American law school is $59,570. At public schools, in-state rates average $32,040. For international students who rarely qualify for in-state pricing, the cost is often higher — and the return on investment increasingly uncertain.

## The Visa Wall

The most cited reason for the pullback is the visa environment. An April report from Shorelight Education found that the United States denied 35 per cent of international student visa applications in 2025 — the highest rejection rate in a decade. Africa and Southeast Asia saw even higher rates, but the chilling effect has spread across all source countries.

International graduate student enrollment was down 12 per cent nationwide in the fall of 2025, according to the Institute of International Education. The J.D. pipeline is softening too: international enrollment in three-year law degree programmes fell nearly 6 per cent in 2025.

Admissions officers, professors, and consultants attribute the trends to a cluster of interconnected pressures: the Trump administration's immigration crackdown, uncertainty over student and work visa availability after graduation, the $100,000 H-1B fee (recently struck down by a federal judge but now being appealed), and a broader rhetorical hostility toward foreign workers that has made prospective students question whether the American credential is worth the risk.

## The UK and Europe Are Winning

The students are not disappearing. They are redirecting.

"I've had people say to me, 'I always wanted to do an LL.M. in the States, but now I want to do it in the UK,'" said Sylvia Polo, an admissions consultant who previously ran LL.M. programmes at Columbia Law School and the University of Miami School of Law.

British and European universities have been aggressively positioning themselves as alternatives. LL.M. programmes in the UK are typically one year and significantly cheaper than their American equivalents. Australia, despite tightening its own student visa rules, remains competitive on cost. And the post-study work visa landscape in the UK — while recently shortened from two years to 18 months for graduates — still offers more certainty than the American H-1B lottery.

For Indian families who have historically viewed an American law degree as the apex of professional credentialing, the calculus is shifting. The degree itself retains its prestige. But the ecosystem around it — the visa, the work authorisation, the political climate — no longer does.

## A Structural Vulnerability

The irony is that American law schools need international students more than ever. Domestic enrollment has been volatile for a decade. Tuition revenue from LL.M. students — who pay full freight and subsidise other programmes — is structurally important to many schools' budgets.

"It's becoming increasingly harder to keep our competitive advantage because of our cost structure and the problem of getting students to want to come to the United States," said Padideh Ala'i, an international law professor at American University in Washington.

Whether this year's decline is a temporary dip or the beginning of a structural contraction depends on factors largely outside the academy's control: visa policy, political rhetoric, and the willingness of the U.S. government to signal that foreign talent is still welcome. On all three fronts, the current trajectory is pointing in the wrong direction.
